Gastroenterology · published research

Colitis

Summary of the Evidence

Thirteen relevant publications were identified: ten animal studies, one older uncontrolled clinical report, one study protocol, and one critical review. One animal publication also includes in-vitro work. The animal literature spans narrow-band photobiomodulation, wavelength comparisons, and broader visible-light exposure, so the interventions are not interchangeable. A recent critical review judged the preclinical findings encouraging but found no eligible clinical treatment evidence (de Souza et al. 2024).

Human and clinical

A database-listed 1999 single-arm report described symptom and colonoscopic improvement after transanal helium-neon laser sessions in 81 people with ulcerative colitis. With no comparison group and no accessible English full text, it cannot establish a treatment effect. A later feasibility protocol studies PBM for fatigue, depression, and pain in inflammatory bowel disease but reports no efficacy results (Ewais et al. 2023).

Animal

Across chemically induced mouse and rat models, PBM studies commonly report lower disease-activity scores, reduced inflammatory markers, improved mucus or barrier measures, and less tissue injury. Two 2023 rat studies found protocol- and sex-dependent responses to local or vascular 660-nm light (Bitencourt et al. 2023; Rodrigues et al. 2023).

Other reports include 830-nm near-infrared treatment, comparisons of blue, red, and green light, and red or 940-nm LED protocols. Outcomes and effective doses differ across models, and broad-spectrum lamp exposure should not be treated as equivalent to narrow-band PBM (Maeng et al. 2026; Zigmond et al. 2014; Belém et al. 2016; Hiratsuka et al. 2014).

In-vitro and ex-vivo

One mixed laboratory and mouse study preconditioned adipose-derived stem cells with PBM before administration. This supports a possible cell-mediated mechanism but does not isolate direct light treatment of the bowel (He et al. 2023).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols range from 660-nm red visible LEDs and 940-nm near-infrared LEDs to 830-nm abdominal irradiation, blue or green visible light, and broad-spectrum lamps. Studies differ in fluence, intensity, treatment frequency, sex, disease model, shaved versus unshaved skin, and local versus vascular delivery. There is no agreed clinical dose or route.

Interpretation

The animal evidence supports further testing because several models show lower inflammation and tissue injury, while also demonstrating that response depends on protocol and model. The single uncontrolled human report is not enough to show that PBM controls colitis in patients. Controlled clinical trials with validated symptoms, endoscopy, medication use, and safety outcomes are needed.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

A 2024 critical review and multiple mouse and rat experiments report favorable short-term disease, tissue, or inflammatory outcomes, but models, wavelengths, doses, delivery routes, and outcomes differ. Human support remains one old uncontrolled report; the later feasibility protocol has no results. Independent replication and controlled patient trials using symptoms and endoscopic outcomes are needed to judge clinical benefit.

Clinical effect estimate

1999 uncontrolled ulcerative-colitis report: 72% of 81 participants reportedly had less pain and less frequent stool after 10–12 transanal helium-neon laser sessions, with mucosal improvement described on colonoscopy. With no comparison group and no accessible English full text, this is an uncontrolled response proportion rather than a treatment-effect estimate.
